Frequently Asked Questions

Can I file a claim if my accident happened in a private parking lot?

Yes. South Carolina negligence law applies to accidents on private property, including parking lots and parking garages. The at-fault driver owes the same duty of care on private property as on a public road. You can pursue an insurance claim or a personal injury lawsuit for injuries sustained in a private parking lot accident.

What if the police refused to come to my parking lot accident?

If police do not respond, document the scene yourself with photographs, collect the other driver's information, identify witnesses, and note whether security cameras were present. You can also file a report at the police station after the fact. The absence of a police report does not prevent you from filing an insurance claim or a lawsuit.

Who is at fault when two cars back into each other in a parking lot?

When two vehicles back out of opposing spaces simultaneously and collide, fault is typically shared. Investigators examine how far each vehicle had traveled, whether either driver had a clearer view, and whether either driver could have stopped to avoid the collision. Under South Carolina's comparative fault rules, each driver's recovery is reduced by their percentage of fault.

Can I sue the parking garage owner for a dangerous condition?

Yes. If a parking garage or lot owner failed to maintain safe conditions -- such as adequate lighting, clear signage, safe ramp design, or properly maintained surfaces -- and that failure contributed to your accident, you may have a premises liability claim against the property owner in addition to any claim against the other driver.

How long do I have to file a parking lot accident claim in South Carolina?

The statute of limitations for personal injury claims in South Carolina is three years from the date of the accident (S.C. Code Section 15-3-530). However, if the parking facility is government-owned, shorter notice deadlines may apply under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act. Contact an attorney promptly to ensure you meet all applicable deadlines.

What compensation can I recover after a parking lot accident?

You may recover compensation for medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, property damage, and future medical costs related to your injuries. If the at-fault party's conduct was reckless -- such as driving while intoxicated in a parking lot -- you may also be entitled to punitive damages under South Carolina law.

Understanding the Tri-County Area: Charleston, Berkeley, and Dorchester

The tri-county region is one of the fastest-growing metropolitan areas in the Southeast, with a combined population exceeding 800,000 residents. The three counties share infrastructure, highway systems, and commuter patterns, but they are legally distinct jurisdictions with separate governance, court systems, and law enforcement agencies. Many residents live in one county, work in another, and travel through a third on their daily commute — which means an accident can occur in a county you may not immediately recognize.

Charleston County is the most populous of the three and encompasses the City of Charleston, Daniel Island, Mount Pleasant, James Island, and West Ashley. It is part of the Ninth Judicial Circuit. Berkeley County covers a vast geographic area north and east of Charleston, including Goose Creek, Hanahan, and Moncks Corner, and falls within the same Ninth Judicial Circuit. Dorchester County includes Summerville, Ladson, and St. George, and is part of the First Judicial Circuit.

This jurisdictional patchwork means that two accidents occurring just miles apart — one on the Charleston County side of I-26 and one on the Dorchester County side — can follow entirely different procedural paths through the court system.

How to Determine Which County Your Accident Occurred In

Identifying the correct county is the first critical step after any accident in the tri-county area. Several methods can help you determine where your crash occurred:

  • The police report — The responding law enforcement agency's report will identify the county and jurisdiction. A report filed by the North Charleston Police Department places the accident in Charleston County, while a Berkeley County Sheriff's Office report confirms a Berkeley County location
  • County boundary markers — Major highways like I-26 and I-526 cross county lines. County boundary signs on interstates and state highways mark where one jurisdiction ends and another begins
  • Address and GPS data — Your vehicle's GPS, smartphone location data, or the address of a nearby business can confirm the county. Mapping applications typically display county boundaries when you search a specific location
  • Mile markers on interstates — Mile marker numbers, combined with South Carolina Department of Transportation maps, can pinpoint the county where an interstate accident occurred

The distinction matters immediately. If your accident occurred on US-78 near Ladson, the county line between Berkeley and Dorchester runs through the area, and the specific location determines which court system has jurisdiction over your claim.

Venue Selection Strategy: Why It Matters More Than You Think

South Carolina venue rules allow personal injury claims to be filed in the county where the accident occurred, the county where the defendant resides, or — for corporate defendants — the county where the corporation maintains a principal place of business or registered agent. This means that in many tri-county accident cases, more than one county may be a proper venue for your lawsuit.

Strategic venue selection is one of the most important early decisions in a personal injury case. An experienced Charleston car accident lawyer will analyze the specific facts of your case and evaluate which county offers the most favorable combination of jury demographics, court calendar speed, judicial tendencies, and procedural rules. Filing in the wrong county can slow your case, reduce your potential recovery, or create unnecessary procedural hurdles.

When the at-fault driver lives in Dorchester County but the accident occurred in Charleston County, your attorney has the option of filing in either jurisdiction. That choice should be made deliberately, based on a careful analysis of how each court system is likely to treat your specific type of case.

Different Court Systems and Jury Pools Across Three Counties

While all three counties apply the same South Carolina substantive law, the practical experience of litigating a case varies significantly from one courthouse to the next.

Charleston County Court of Common Pleas

Charleston County handles the highest volume of civil cases in the tri-county area. The jury pool draws from the City of Charleston, Mount Pleasant, Daniel Island, James Island, and surrounding areas. Charleston County juries tend to include a diverse mix of urban professionals, service industry workers, and retirees. The court's docket is among the busiest in the state, which can mean longer wait times for trial dates but also creates pressure on defendants to settle rather than face extended litigation.

Berkeley County Court of Common Pleas

Berkeley County's jury pool draws from communities like Goose Creek, Hanahan, Moncks Corner, and the rapidly growing residential developments north of the Cooper River. Berkeley County has experienced explosive population growth in recent years, shifting its jury demographics from a predominantly rural pool to an increasingly suburban one. The court typically moves cases through its docket somewhat faster than Charleston County due to lower overall volume.

Dorchester County Court of Common Pleas

Dorchester County draws jurors from Summerville, Ladson, St. George, and surrounding communities. Dorchester is part of the First Judicial Circuit (shared with Orangeburg County), which means the judges who preside over cases rotate between the two counties. The jury pool in Dorchester County reflects a mix of suburban Summerville residents and more rural communities in the western part of the county.

These differences in jury composition and court procedures can influence everything from mediation outcomes to trial verdicts. Insurance companies track verdict data by county and adjust their settlement offers based on where they believe the case will be tried.

Which Law Enforcement Agency Investigates Your Accident

The law enforcement agency that responds to and investigates your accident depends on both the county and the specific municipality where the crash occurred. Understanding this matters because the quality and thoroughness of the accident investigation can significantly impact your ability to prove fault.

  • Charleston County — The Charleston Police Department handles crashes within the City of Charleston, the North Charleston Police Department covers North Charleston, the Mount Pleasant Police Department responds to crashes in Mount Pleasant, and the Charleston County Sheriff's Office covers unincorporated areas
  • Berkeley County — The Goose Creek Police Department, Hanahan Police Department, and Berkeley County Sheriff's Office each handle crashes in their respective jurisdictions
  • Dorchester County — The Summerville Police Department covers the Town of Summerville, while the Dorchester County Sheriff's Office handles unincorporated areas including Ladson
  • South Carolina Highway Patrol — SCHP investigates accidents on interstates and state highways across all three counties, and also responds to crashes in unincorporated areas

Different agencies use different reporting formats, have different levels of staffing for accident reconstruction, and vary in how thoroughly they document the scene. In complex or high-severity cases, it is critical to preserve all available evidence early — before reports are finalized and physical evidence is lost.

Government Liability Differences by County

When a government entity bears responsibility for the conditions that caused your accident — a poorly maintained road, a malfunctioning traffic signal, a missing stop sign — the claims process depends on which government body is responsible for that infrastructure.

In South Carolina, the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code Section 15-78-10 et seq.) governs claims against state and local government entities. The Act waives sovereign immunity in certain circumstances but imposes strict requirements, including a damages cap and mandatory notice provisions. You must serve written notice on the governmental entity before filing suit, and the procedural requirements differ depending on whether the responsible entity is the South Carolina Department of Transportation (SCDOT), a county government, or a municipality.

A pothole on a county-maintained road in Berkeley County requires notice to the Berkeley County government. A malfunctioning traffic signal maintained by the Town of Summerville in Dorchester County requires notice to the municipal government. A dangerous condition on I-26 — which runs through all three counties — requires a claim against SCDOT regardless of which county the accident occurred in. Identifying the correct government entity and serving proper notice within the required timeframe is essential, and getting it wrong can destroy an otherwise valid claim.

Comparative Fault: South Carolina vs. Georgia Rules

South Carolina applies a modified comparative fault rule under which an injured plaintiff can recover damages as long as their own fault does not reach 51 percent. If you are found 50 percent or less at fault, your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault. If you are found 51 percent or more at fault, you recover nothing. This standard applies uniformly across Charleston, Berkeley, and Dorchester counties.

Georgia applies a similar but slightly stricter version of modified comparative fault under O.C.G.A. Section 51-12-33. In Georgia, a plaintiff is barred from recovery if they are 50 percent or more at fault — meaning a plaintiff who is exactly 50 percent at fault recovers nothing in Georgia but could still recover in South Carolina. For individuals who travel between the two states or have connections to both, understanding which state's law applies to their accident is critical.

In tri-county accident cases, comparative fault becomes particularly relevant at intersections where both drivers claim the other was at fault. The jury's allocation of fault percentages — and the county where the jury is seated — can make the difference between a full recovery, a reduced recovery, and no recovery at all.

Filing Deadlines You Cannot Afford to Miss

The statute of limitations for personal injury claims differs between South Carolina and Georgia, and missing the deadline eliminates your right to recover compensation entirely:

  • South Carolina: You have 3 years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit (S.C. Code Section 15-3-530)
  • Georgia: You have 2 years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit (O.C.G.A. Section 9-3-33)

For accidents in the tri-county area, the South Carolina three-year statute applies. However, shorter deadlines may apply in specific situations. Claims against government entities under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act require earlier notice. Claims involving minors or incapacitated individuals may have tolling provisions that extend the deadline. And if your case involves a defendant who flees the state, the statute may be tolled during their absence.

Regardless of the statutory deadline, the practical reality is that evidence degrades over time. Surveillance footage is overwritten, witnesses forget details, and vehicle damage is repaired. The sooner you begin building your case, the stronger your evidence will be when it matters.
